stories.title: Injuries as violence erupts at South Africa anti-migrant protest
stories.summary: A demonstration against undocumented migrants in South Africa descended into violence Thursday with one foreign national arrested and a community leader saying five Congolese were hurt. The protest was in the port city of Durban which has been at the epicentre of weeks of action against irregular migration in which at least four foreign nationals have been killed and tens of thousands have fled the country. Police said about 100 marchers from an anti-illegal migrant group went on what they called "a clean-up campaign" against an encampment of several hundred foreign nationals outside a government office. Foreigners, many of them from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), moved to the site 13 weeks ago to seek protection against mobs of South Africans campaigning against undocumented migrants. "During the commotion, stones were thrown around, and one which was thrown by a foreign national landed on a police officer," police said. The person was arrested, a statement said, without giving details. A leader of the group of foreigners told AFP that five Congolese nationals including two children were hurt in the clash. "The march today was very violent," said Bishop Raphael, who is from the DRC. "They found us here and immediately attacked our people. We are not committing any crime by being here. This is uncalled for," he said. Many of the people in the group claim to be refugees from the DRC.

stories.title: Milei touts 'winds of change' as he reasserts Argentina's claim to the Falklands
stories.summary: It comes after US President Donald Trump cast doubt on US support for the UK in a potential conflict over the territory, pointing to Britain's lack of backing in the Iran war. Argentine President Javier Milei said on Thursday that "winds of change" were beginning to favour Argentina's claim to the Falkland Islands. In a TV address, the right-wing leader touted US President Donald Trump's recent suggestion that Washington could reconsider its neutral position on the islands, which have been at the centre of a long running and bloody dispute between Argentina and the United Kingdom. "President Trump recently stated that the United States is reevaluating its historical position regarding Las Malvinas," Milei said, using the Argentine name for the islands. "This threat is not to be taken lightly," he continued, adding: "Winds of change are blowing across the world in favor of our cause." Trump had earlier this week cast doubt on US support for the UK in a potential conflict over the territory, pointing to Britain's lack of backing in the Iran war - which began in late February following US and Israeli strikes on Iran. "Your country is not doing well," he told GB News. "Don't forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the Strait of Hormuz, and you weren't there to help me. Your country was not there to help me". In his speech, Milei also announced that he would be signing off on a series of new sanctions targeting oil companies working off of the islands, which he described as "under British occupation." "For 50 years, the United Nations has called on Argentina and the United Kingdom to refrain from taking unilateral actions regarding the territory, including the exploitation of its natural resources, until the dispute is resolved. However, the United Kingdom has systematically failed to comply with this call," he said.

stories.title: Gwangju Biennale chief regrets China's withdrawal over Taiwan row
stories.summary: The chief executive of the Gwangju Biennale on Friday expressed regret over the withdrawal of Chinese artists from the art festival following a dispute over the naming of a Taiwan exhibition space. Youn Bum-mo, the chief executive of the South Korean contemporary art exhibition, said he had wanted the artists to participate in the Chinese Pavilion until the last minute but was disappointed they ultimately pulled out. He described the situation as "apologetic and saddened," during a press conference to mark the exhibition's opening in Gwangju, located some 270 kilometers south of Seoul. The 16th edition of the biennale, one of Asia's most prominent contemporary art events, was scheduled to open with a ceremony later Friday for a 72-day run through Nov. 5. It features a main exhibition alongside a pavilion project, launched in 2018, that allows national and institutional participants to present separate shows. This year, organizers had planned to host 16 national pavilions and 11 institutional pavilions, including one by National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts (NTMoFA). However, tensions arose after the Gwangju Biennale Foundation, which operates the exhibition, initially agreed to refer to the space as the "Taiwan Pavilion" before changing it to the "NTMoFA Pavilion," prompting a protest from Taiwan's culture ministry. The foundation later reversed its decision and approved the use of "Taiwan Pavilion" to ensure the exhibition could proceed smoothly. The move then drew a formal expression of regret and concern from Chinese Ambassador to South Korea Dai Bing to the mayor of the Jeonnam-Gwangju Special Metropolitan City, Min Hyung-bae. Artists representing the China Pavilion subsequently halted installation work and withdrew from the event in protest. China views the self-governing democracy as part of its own territory under a one-China principle. During the press conference, Youn explained that the original applicant for the pavilion was an institution rather than the Taiwanese government.
